Y1L1.if_not: No prerequisite: teach as written, as every class starts here.
Y1L1.adds: Pupils learn that some machines do the same every time while others guess, and the guessing ones use AI. They can sort everyday machines and give a reason.
Y1L1.prep: Bleep: a robot puppet, soft toy or decorated box. Mystery Bag: a pillowcase or drawstring bag holding, in this order: a torch; the smart speaker card; a calculator; the photos app card; a toy toaster (or its card); the video app card; a musical push button toy; the phone card. Print and cut out slide 16 for the cards, and use the real thing wherever you have it. Signs: print slide 17 and stick "Same every time" and "Makes a guess" on opposite walls. Optional: a floor robot such as a Bee-Bot for slide 12. Own It: plain paper and crayons. Test the torch and the calculator before the lesson.
Y1L1.need: Bleep, a mystery bag of everyday objects, printed cards and signs (slides 16 and 17)
Y1L1.exit: 1. What is a guess? 2. Thumbs up or thumbs down: does a torch make a guess? 3. A camera at the door says "It's Grandma!" Does it make a guess? How do you know?
Y1L1.look_for: pupils who give a reason ("it has to guess what I said") rather than just a group, and pupils who stop quickly and join in when the IDEAL sign appears.
Y1L1.time: 60 minutes (45 minutes: shorten the edges and keep the middle. Ask two Remember When questions, keep Link It to 2 minutes, the IDEAL Check to 2 minutes and the full exit ticket to 3 minutes. Y2L4.if_not: If Y1L6 was missed, Q4 is new: show the Never tell cards on Y1L6 slide 8, about 3 minutes.
Y2L4.adds: Pupils learn what personal information is and the routine Stop, Keep it, Tell when a machine asks for it.
Y2L4.prep: Print slide 16 (room signs), on A3 if you can, and stick Safe to Say and Keep to Myself on opposite sides of the room with a clear path between. Print slide 17 (Bleep's question cards): one set for you to read from and one set per table for pupils who sort at their seats. Have your Bleep ready. Plain paper and colouring pencils for Own It. Read the safeguarding row above and know who your Designated Safeguarding Lead is today.
Y2L4.safeguarding: What could come up. Talking about private information and machines that ask questions can prompt pupils to mention being asked for photos or personal details in games or apps, contact from people they do not know, older siblings' devices, or worries at home. A small number of pupils may have particular reasons why where they live or their name must be kept private (for example looked after children or families fleeing harm), so the lesson never asks anyone to share real details. How to handle it. Never ask pupils to say or write their real address, full name, school name or passwords: they sort questions, they do not answer them, and the shield uses pictures only. If a pupil discloses something that worries you, listen calmly, do not promise to keep it secret, do not ask leading questions, and pass it on to your Designated Safeguarding Lead the same day using your school's procedures. Distinguish private (our information) from secrets: pupils should never keep a secret that makes them feel worried or uncomfortable. Data protection. Never enter pupils' personal information into any AI tool or online service.
Y2L4.need: Printed room signs (slide 16) and question cards (slide 17), Bleep, paper, colouring pencils
Y2L4.exit: 1. Bleep asks where you live. Safe to Say or Keep to Myself? 2. A game asks "What is your school called?" Safe to Say or Keep to Myself? How do you know? 3. A game asks for your password. What do you do?
Y2L4.look_for: pupils who use the test (does it tell someone who I am or where to find me?) rather than guessing, who say the routine without prompting, and who can name a grown-up to tell.

Y6L1.safeguarding: What could come up: pupils may mention fake or nude images they have seen or been sent, images of classmates or staff, scams on family phones, or upsetting content from older siblings' devices. Never show harmful fakes. This lesson describes real, child appropriate examples instead. Do not search for or display deepfakes live, and never ask pupils to make, find or share images of real people. If a pupil discloses that an image of them or another child has been made or shared: stay calm, listen, do not promise secrecy, reassure them it is not their fault, and report to your DSL straight away, following your school's child protection policy and Keeping children safe in education. Do not view, copy, screenshot, print or forward the image, and do not ask the pupil to show it to you; the DSL decides every next step, including deletion. The government's UKCIS advice, Sharing nudes and semi-nudes: advice for education settings (updated March 2024), covers AI-generated and digitally altered images and sets out what to do. The DSL may also point families to Childline and the IWF's Report Remove service. The law, for your awareness only (not for the slides): any indecent image of a child, including an AI-generated or computer-made one, is illegal to make, possess or share. This includes images made with "nudify" apps that turn an ordinary photo into a fake nude, which pupils of this age may hear about or be sent. Sharing a sexually explicit image of an adult without consent, including a deepfake, has been an offence in England and Wales since 31 January 2024 (Online Safety Act 2023). Creating one, or asking someone else to create one, became an offence on 6 February 2026 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 138). The Crime and Policing Act 2026 (Royal Assent 29 April 2026) adds offences covering image generators designed to produce child sexual abuse images and tools that make fake intimate images; ask your DSL which parts are in force. Personal data: never enter pupils' names, photos or voices into any AI tool. In the lesson: if a pupil starts to describe something upsetting or unsuitable, thank them, move the class on, and speak to them privately afterwards. On slide 14, keep the discussion about everyday jokes and kindness, and do not discuss or describe sexual deepfakes. If a pupil raises them, say calmly that making or sharing images like that is never OK and can be against the law, that it is never the fault of the person in the picture, and that a trusted adult will help, even if they have already seen or shared one. Then follow up privately and through your DSL.

understand: Everything taught in Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit. This is the end of unit assessment: pupils use that learning on their own.

before.adds: Pupils apply the whole unit independently, which gives the evidence for the tracker.

1.starting_point: No earlier IDEAL Thinkers teaching; pupils bring home, Nursery and Reception experience of machines, guessing, patterns and sorting.
first_time: Year 1 is the entry point, so no earlier learning is assumed.
Say plainly on Y1L1 slide 5 that Bleep is pretend.
None needed: Y1L1 is designed as the first lesson.
A school adopting with Year 1 follows the unit exactly as written.
journey: L1: some machines guess, and those use AI.
L2: AI learns from lots of different examples.
L3: the AI Loop; a person checks the guess.

L3: guessing AI tools make things accessible, and people check them.
L4: ask for a hint, not the answer.
L5: say honestly when AI helped.
L6: design a Helpful Feed using the whole unit.

4.starting_point: Pupils bring AI learning from examples and guessing from patterns, people checking, privacy and Keep to Myself, Hint, not answer, being honest, and people choosing the words for AI.
